title: Charlie Kirk's Killing And The Alarming Rise Of Political Violence In America | Explained | Explainers News - News18
text: The killing of American conservative activist Charlie Kirk has once again thrust political violence in the United States into the spotlight. On Thursday, Kirk, 31, was shot in the neck while speaking outdoors at Utah Valley University as part of his American Comeback Tour. His appearance had already drawn controversy after nearly 1,000 people signed a petition to block him from the campus, citing what they described as divisive rhetoric. Kirk was known for courting controversy on college campuses, including a recent claim that “young women who voted for Kamala Harris, they want careerism, consumerism and loneliness." As Kirk addressed the crowd, he collapsed mid-sentence after being struck by a bullet . Utah’s Republican governor Spencer Cox called the killing a “political assassination". President Donald Trump, a close ally of Kirk, described him as “great and even legendary" while ordering flags to be flown at half-mast. Kirk’s assassination, carried out in front of students at a university event meant for political debate, has intensified concerns that political disagreement in America is increasingly being settled through violence rather than words. Kirk’s assassination is not an isolated act. It comes after years of incidents showing how threats and attacks against politicians, judges, and activists have become a recurring feature of American life. In July 2024, Trump was wounded in the ear during a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, when a gunman opened fire, killing a spectator. A second attempt came weeks later when a man was arrested for allegedly hiding at Trump’s Florida golf course with a rifle. Governors, too, have faced danger. Earlier this year, Pennsylvania governor Josh Shapiro’s residence was set ablaze in an arson attack while his family was inside. In 2020, Michigan governor Gretchen Whitmer was the target of a foiled kidnapping plot by anti-government extremists. Judges, too, are increasingly under siege. In December 2024, Chief Justice John Roberts, head of the US Supreme Court, warned of a “significant uptick" in threats, with the US Marshals Service investigating more than 1,000 serious cases in five years. This string of violent episodes points to a deeper problem: the normalisation of political violence across the ideological spectrum. As former Democratic congresswoman Gabrielle Giffords, herself a survivor of a 2011 assassination attempt, put it: “Democratic societies will always have political disagreements, but we must never allow America to become a country that confronts those disagreements with violence." The modern era of political assassinations in the US can be traced back to high-profile shootings of public figures. In 2011, Giffords was shot in the head during a meeting with constituents in Arizona. Six people were killed and 13 others wounded in that attack. In 2017, Republican lawmaker from Louisiana, Steve Scalise was nearly killed when a gunman opened fire during a congressional baseball practice. Scalise, now House Majority Leader, invoked his own experience after Kirk’s death: “There’s no excuse for political violence in our country. It’s got to end." More recently, the violence has spread beyond Washington. In June 2025, Minnesota state’s former House Speaker Emerita Melissa Hortman and her husband were killed in their home by a man disguised as a police officer. The same attacker also shot state senator John Hoffman and his wife, who survived. Acting US Attorney Joe Thompson called the murders “targeted political assassinations the likes of which have never been seen in Minnesota." From national leaders to governors and state legislators, the range of targets has widened. Kirk’s killing shows that even campus speaking events have now become sites of deadly political violence. Reactions in the US capital revealed just how polarised the political climate has become. A moment of silence for Kirk in the House of Representatives descended into shouting after Republican lawmaker Lauren Boebert urged prayers, quipping “Silent prayers get silent results." Democrats objected, asking why other killings were not receiving the same attention. What followed was swearing, finger-pointing and a call from the floor to “pass a gun law". At the White House, mourning was mixed with anger. Trump posted on Truth Social calling Kirk “one of America’s greatest champions" and, in a video address, blamed the “radical left" for fuelling violence. He vowed to hold to account not only perpetrators but also organisations accused of supporting violent protests. Democrats, meanwhile, offered more muted responses. As reported by the Financial Times , Barack Obama condemned the “despicable violence" but cautioned against politicising it before more details were known. California governor Gavin Newsom labelled the act “disgusting" while George W Bush, the former Republican president, urged Americans to remember that “members of other political parties are not our enemies; they are our fellow citizens." But online reactions were starkly divided. Trump adviser Stephen Miller and entrepreneur Elon Musk accused liberals of having “blood on their hands," while Illinois governor JB Pritzker directly criticised Trump’s rhetoric for “fomenting" violence. The scale of the threat is reflected in official data. US Capitol Police investigated 9,474 threats and concerning statements against lawmakers in 2024, nearly matching the record high of 9,625 in 2021. The wider toll of gun violence is staggering. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 46,728 people died from gun violence in 2023, the third-highest annual figure ever recorded. Surveys suggest attitudes towards political violence are hardening. A Reuters/Ipsos poll of 2024 found only 6 per cent of Americans believed it acceptable to threaten political opponents. But research led by Robert Pape, a political scientist who directs the Chicago Project on Security and Threats at the University of Chicago, painted a far more troubling picture. In May 2025, his team found about 40 per cent of Democrats supported using force to remove Trump from the presidency, while about 25 per cent of Republicans supported deploying the military to stop protests against Trump’s agenda, findings he detailed in The New York Times . Speaking to The Guardian , Pape warned this reflects an “era of violent populism." Experts warn that the aftermath of Kirk’s death could deepen America’s political crisis rather than calm it. Progressive commentator Hasan Piker, a left-leaning livestreamer with a large online following, described the shooting as a “terrifying incident," warning on his livestream that the “reverberation of people seeking out vengeance in the aftermath of this violent, abhorrent incident is going to be genuinely worrisome." Within hours, right-wing influencers were already using the language of retribution — the prominent account Libs of TikTok declared simply: “THIS IS WAR." Sociologists argue that this rhetoric, layered on top of a history of recent assassinations and attempts, risks inflaming an already combustible environment. Ruth Braunstein, a professor of sociology at Johns Hopkins University, told Reuters that Kirk’s killing “has the capacity to further inflame a political environment where the temperature is already way too high." Political assassinations have punctuated American history, from Abraham Lincoln in 1865 to John F Kennedy, Robert Kennedy and Martin Luther King Jr in the 1960s. Ronald Reagan also survived an attempt in 1981. The recent litany — Giffords in 2011, Scalise in 2017, Trump in 2024, Hortman in 2025, and now Kirk — has left lawmakers pleading for change. Christian Heyne of the Brady gun-control group said: “Gun violence doesn’t check party ID. It is indiscriminate. And the American people always lose." Senator Thom Tillis urged restraint: “Every single person who encourages aggressive responses rather than civil discourse owns a certain amount of responsibility." But with Washington mired in division, and rhetoric escalating on both sides, meaningful reform looks elusive. For now, America remains caught in a cycle of shock, outrage and blame, and the call that “it’s got to end" sounds more urgent than ever.
